notes: \cpara{The epigraph is the first sentence of Gilbert and Malone's abstract, quoted exactly. Their definition limits the bias to behaviour that the situation could ``entirely'' explain.}
\cpara{Illustrates with a kick at a vending machine: seen from outside, an angry person; seen from inside, a bad day.}
\cpara{Explains the difference: an observer does not see the actor's history. This is the first of the four causes Gilbert and Malone describe, ``lack of awareness'' of the situation.}

\cfact{Stated as a general rule, and the evidence available when the post was written was weaker. Malle's meta-analysis of 173 published studies of this self-other difference (\textsc{Psychological Bulletin}, November 2006) found ``average effect sizes from d = -0.016 to d = 0.095,'' close to zero. The difference held for negative events, such as the post's kick, and reversed for positive ones.}

\cpara{Argues from prior probability: late buses are commoner than people born with extreme anger, just as any given stretch of DNA is unlikely to carry one of a person's few mutations. The mutation figure comes with ``If I recall correctly'' and no source.}

\clogic{The comparison is set against an extreme disposition, a ``mutant.'' The judgment ``an angry person'' can mean less: someone more irritable than most, which is common. Against that milder rival, the comparison with late buses does not settle the question.}

\cpara{Cites the classic experiment of Jones and Harris (1967). The hedged summary, that people ``don't seem to properly discount,'' fits the result as Gilbert and Malone report it: observers inferred attitudes from essays written under instruction, though ``much weaker'' ones than from essays freely chosen.}

\cfact{The topic was Fidel Castro, not abortion. Gilbert and Malone (p.~24) describe ``essays that supported or opposed Cuba's president, Fidel Castro,'' written by an essayist ``instructed by his debate coach'' to take a side. Wikipedia's account says the side was set by a coin toss. I could not read the 1967 paper to settle how the side was assigned.}

\cpara{Offers a cause of the bias: essences are easier to think of than mechanisms. The cause is the post's own and comes without evidence. Gilbert and Malone, whom the post cites, describe four causes, and this is not among them; they also write (p.~22) that there is ``still no single, widely accepted explanation'' of the bias. The general claim about essences returns in ``Mysterious Answers to Mysterious Questions'' (see the note there).}
\cpara{Adds two related effects: false consensus, with an example about drinking students given without a source, and the fundamental attribution error.}

\cfact{This joins two ideas. Lee Ross, who named the fundamental attribution error in 1977, meant the tendency to underestimate the power of situations (Gilbert and Malone, p.~24). ``Reversing this tendency for ourselves'' is a separate claim, Jones and Nisbett's actor-observer hypothesis (1971), the one tested in Malle's meta-analysis noted above.}
\cpara{States the lesson: assume that people see themselves as behaving normally, and ask what situation they think they are in. The last sentence grants that dispositions exist.}
\cpara{A thought experiment built to have one sensible answer: a button that destroys the world, and one that stops it.}

\cpara{Applies the lesson to the author: given the author's view of the situation, wanting to save the world needs no special explanation. Footnote 4 points to the author's chapter on AI risk for that view.}

\cpara{Grants that the beliefs, not the reaction, are what call for explanation, and raises false consensus against the author's own case. The answer to that doubt is a bet (``I'd still bet''), not evidence.}
\cpara{Concludes that even people who do terrible things see themselves as normal, and are not ``exceptional mutants.''}
\clogic{Stated here without exception. The next day's post, ``Are Your Enemies Innately Evil?'', makes one: ``true psychopaths.''}
